title: Reachy Mini: the $300 open source robot you can actually hack — Andres Marafioti, Hugging Face

primary.label: Multimodal & Realtime Systems
primary.rationale: The talk’s spine is a realtime voice-and-vision loop on an embodied robot: VAD, streaming Parakeet STT, LLM tool use of camera and motion, Coqui TTS, echo cancellation, and face tracking. That is multimodal/realtime systems, not a text-only agent or a generic platform pitch.

secondary.label: Inference & Model Systems
secondary.rationale: The longest technical section is serving: HF Inference Endpoints, a load balancer over a 7,500-robot fleet, separated LLM nodes, plus making TTS stream with a static KV cache and CUDA graph captures to move realtime factor from 0.8 to 5.8.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: Reachy Mini is framed as an open-source substrate for hackers and schools—software tools, hosted endpoints, vibe-codable apps in Python/Java/HTML—not a single end-user robot product.

secondary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
secondary.rationale: Non-humanoid cute morphology, unassembled shipping as pedagogy, voice as the interface, and “make the interaction communal” are product and human-factors claims that structure the first half.

domains.label: Robotics & Embodied
domains.rationale: The object of the talk is a physical desktop robot, a shipped fleet, and stacked arms/mobile base—not a purely software assistant.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The audience is technical builders; the offer is open-source software, HF endpoints, and vibe-codable apps on the robot or a laptop.

domains.label: Education & Learning
domains.rationale: The $300 SKU is sold in bulk to high schools and universities so students can experiment; unassembled shipping is itself a teaching device.

summary:
Andy Marafioti opens by introducing himself as the lead of multimodal research at Hugging Face and previewing Reachy Mini (ASR repeatedly renders the name as “Richie Mini” / “Richy Mini”). He sketches the state of robotics: humanoids are advancing quickly—he recently watched a boxing match at a Zurich robotics club—and companies are selling home robots and robotaxis (he mentions Waymo in London). Those machines are still mid five-figure (about $50K) for humanoids and six figures for Waymo-class vehicles. They imitate humans rather than invent new morphologies, are too expensive for a high school to buy ten of, are hard to adapt, target companies, and do not invite a personal connection.

Voice AI, by contrast, is mature. Commercial systems (a Paris voice-agent shop he calls “Rhodium,” GPT realtime, Siri) and open models (Mistral’s talk, an ASR-garbled “Box Rally,” tiny Kokoro/“Cocoro” at 80M parameters, Hugging Face speech-to-speech pipelines) already exist. Almost no one is working on how people will talk to the coming robots. Hugging Face’s answer is Reachy Mini: an affordable, repairable, hackable, cute, non-humanoid expressive robot aimed at people who already have a computer. Units ship unassembled so the owner learns to repair anything that later breaks. Two SKUs: $450 with a Raspberry Pi and battery, and $300 without, sold in bulk to schools. Community hacks include 3D-printed Halloween parts and petting-to-purr interactions. A recorded demo shows the robot answering, taking a photo, describing a selfie, and performing a happiness emotion, with a running lobster gag.

Everything—models, agents, software—is open source. They have shipped 7,500 robots; conversation is by far the most used app. Because many users are GPU-poor, Hugging Face hosts the stack. Three layers: (1) the on-robot conversation app handles microphone/speakers, echo cancellation, tool dispatch for motion and emotion, and camera/face tracking; (2) a speech-to-speech pipeline Marafioti has maintained at Hugging Face for two years: VAD, Parakeet STT with partials every 150ms, an LLM that can tool-call movement or camera, then Coqui TTS; (3) Hugging Face Inference Endpoints behind a load balancer, with LLM inference (ASR: “Coqui 3.5 27B”) scaled separately from conversation nodes so chatty vs silent robots do not share one latency budget.

The technical centerpiece is making Coqui 3 TTS fast enough for voice agents. The released model matched paper quality but not claimed latency: it generated the full utterance before emitting audio, and the autoregressive loop did 500 CPU–GPU synchronized steps per audio packet because of a dynamic KV cache. He added streaming, switched to a static KV cache, and used CUDA graph captures. Realtime factor went from 0.8 (1.2s to generate 1s) to 5.8 (~200ms per second of audio); time-to-first-audio fell from several seconds to milliseconds. A Hugging Face Space demo clones voices in realtime. He stresses that infrastructure time can equal model time once the model is fast. He wants people to own the interaction model—vibe-code apps from the repo, run GPU-less apps on-device or on a laptop, in Java, Python, or HTML. Q&A covers on-robot apps, stacking SO-100/SO-101 arms and a Kiwi three-wheel base, and remaining TTS corner cases versus Coqui’s faster hosted API.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Reachy Mini is Hugging Face’s $300–$450 open-source desktop robot for hackers, students, and researchers—not a $50K humanoid.
Voice AI is already mature; the missing work is how people will talk to incoming robots.
The robot is non-humanoid, ships unassembled, and is meant to be repaired and 3D-printed on by its owner.
Conversation software, models, and agents are open source; 7,500 units have shipped and talking is the most used app.
Serving has three layers: on-robot conversation app, speech-to-speech pipeline, and Hugging Face Inference Endpoints with a load balancer.
STT is Parakeet at 150ms partials; the LLM can tool-call motion and camera; TTS is Coqui/Kokoro.
LLM inference is scaled separately from conversation nodes so mixed talkativeness does not spike latency.
Faster Coqui 3 TTS used streaming, a static KV cache, and CUDA graphs to move realtime factor from 0.8 to 5.8.
Infrastructure latency can equal model latency once TTS is fast; both must be designed for voice agents.
The goal is communal, vibe-codeable robot interaction, including stacking SO-100/SO-101 arms and a Kiwi wheeled base.

sections.title: Introduction and the expensive humanoid status quo
sections.summary: Andy Marafioti (Hugging Face multimodal research) introduces Reachy Mini. Humanoids and home robots are advancing fast but cost $50K+ and imitate humans rather than invent new forms, so schools cannot prototype with them.

sections.title: Voice AI is mature; robot conversation is not
sections.summary: Commercial and open voice agents already work (GPT realtime, Siri, Hugging Face speech-to-speech, tiny Kokoro). Almost no one is designing how people will talk to incoming robots; Reachy Mini is aimed at hackers and students.

sections.title: Reachy Mini product: cheap, cute, unassembled, hackable
sections.summary: The robot is expressive but non-humanoid, ships unassembled so owners can repair it, and is sold as $450 (Pi + battery) or $300 bulk school units. Community hacks include 3D-printed parts and pet-to-purr interactions.

sections.title: Conversation demo and 7,500-unit open-source fleet
sections.summary: A recorded demo shows talk, photo, scene description, and emotion. Software, models, and agents are open source. 7,500 units have shipped; conversation is the most used app; many users cannot host the models locally.

sections.title: Three-layer serving: on-robot app, S2S pipeline, HF endpoints
sections.summary: On-robot app does echo cancellation, motion/emotion tools, and face tracking. Mid layer is a two-year HF speech-to-speech pipeline (VAD, Parakeet 150ms, LLM tools, Coqui TTS). Cloud layer is HF Inference Endpoints with a load balancer and separately scaled LLM nodes.

sections.title: Making Coqui 3 TTS fast enough for voice agents
sections.summary: Released Coqui 3 TTS matched quality but not claimed speed: no streaming, 500 CPU–GPU steps, dynamic KV cache. Streaming + static KV cache + CUDA graphs moved RTF from 0.8 to 5.8 and TTFA to milliseconds. A HF Space demo is public; infrastructure time still matters.

sections.title: Communal interaction, vibe coding, and Q&A
sections.summary: He wants robot interaction developed by everyone, not gated by $50K hardware. Apps can be vibe-coded and run on-robot or on a laptop. Q&A covers plugins, SO-100/SO-101 arms plus Kiwi wheeled base, and remaining TTS corner cases versus Coqui’s hosted API.

demonstrations: Recorded phone demo: Reachy Mini greets, tells a lobster joke, takes a photo, describes a hotel-room selfie, and shows a happiness emotion
Architecture walkthrough of VAD → Parakeet STT → LLM tools → Coqui TTS plus on-robot conversation app and HF endpoints
TTS optimization story: non-streaming output, 500-step CPU–GPU loop, static KV cache, CUDA graphs, RTF 0.8 → 5.8
Hugging Face Space demo of faster Coqui 3 TTS cloning voices and speaking pasted text in realtime
On-stage idle motion app one-shotted from the robot repo via vibe coding
limitations: ASR is noisy on product names: Reachy Mini rendered as Richie/Richy Mini; Andres as Andy; Kokoro as Cocoro; likely Qwen/CosyVoice/Coqui confusion on the 27B LLM and “Coqui 3 TTS”
The live robot conversation is shown as a pre-recorded phone video, not a stage live demo
Serving architecture is described at slide depth without published latency SLOs or cost figures for the 7,500-unit fleet
“Rhodium in Paris” and “Box Rally” are not resolved from the transcript alone
SO-100/SO-101 + Kiwi stacking is designed but he has not yet seen it done in the wild
quantitativeClaims: Humanoid robots are mid five-figure, at least $50K; Waymo-class vehicles are mid six figures
Reachy Mini SKUs are $450 (Pi + battery) and $300 (bulk school unit)
Kokoro/Cocoro is cited at 80 million parameters
Parakeet partial transcripts are sent every 150 milliseconds
The LLM named in ASR is Coqui 3.5 27B (likely a Qwen/Qwen3-class 27B; treat as ASR-noisy)
Original TTS did 500 autoregressive steps per audio packet
Realtime factor moved from 0.8 (1.2s per 1s audio) to 5.8 (~200ms per 1s audio)
Time-to-first-audio fell from several seconds to a few milliseconds; the Space demo claims first-token latency under 200ms and ~4x realtime
Q&A leftover time was 1 minute 57 seconds

organization.name: Hugging Face
organization.summary: Hugging Face is an independent company whose homepage describes it as the AI community building the future: a collaboration platform for models, datasets, and applications. Andres (Andy) Marafioti, the speaker, leads multimodal research there (HF profile andito). Hugging Face publishes official Reachy Mini documentation and the hf.co/reachy-mini product page (branded Powered by Hugging Face), hosts the conversation fleet on Inference Endpoints, and blogs about the local conversation stack. Hardware/SDK repositories are published by Pollen Robotics with the same Hugging Face branding; that is a partner publishing relationship, not a rename.
organization.status: Independent open-source AI platform as of the research date. Homepage, org profile, Reachy Mini docs, and hf.co/reachy-mini remain live. Current list prices on the product page are $499 Wireless / $399 Lite versus the talk’s $450 / $300. Pollen Robotics remains the GitHub/store publisher of the SDK and kits.
